SqlVector.summary: Represents a vector value in SQL Server.

remarks.para: The type parameter determines the vector's base type: corresponds to float32, and corresponds to float16. No other type is supported.

is not available on .NET Framework, so SqlVector<Half> cannot be used there. A float16 column can still be read on .NET Framework, either as a JSON array through the string read paths, or as a SqlVector<float>, which widens the elements to single precision. Widening is exact, so no information is lost. Values can be written to a float16 column from .NET Framework as a JSON string, or as a SqlVector<float>, which the server converts. Native float32 writes support at most 1,998 elements. To write wider float16 vectors, up to 3,996 elements, bind the JSON string as varchar(max) instead.

A float16 column is returned in its binary form when Vector Type Support=v2 is configured and version 2 is negotiated with the server. The keyword defaults to v1, which supports native float32 only. Under v1 or off, a float16 column is returned as varchar(max) containing a JSON array.

On .NET Framework, float16 workloads do more work per value than they do on .NET. Because isn't available, the driver widens each element to single precision when it reads a float16 column, and renders the result as a JSON array for the string read paths. On .NET, a SqlVector<Half> wraps the payload the server sent, so no per-element conversion takes place. If you read float16 columns in bulk on .NET Framework, prefer GetSqlVector<float> over the string read paths: both widen the elements, but only the string paths also serialize the result.

Conversion between base types is performed by SQL Server, which reports an error if a value is outside the range the destination can represent. Converting from float32 to float16 loses precision for values which the narrower type cannot represent exactly, in the same way as inserting a JSON literal does.

Bulk copy preserves the base type of native vector sources in its incoming declaration and payload. SQL Server converts the value to the destination column's base type. JSON text copied into a float16 column is sent as varchar(max), so SQL Server performs its parsing and rounding too. The existing JSON-to-float32 bulk-copy conversion is unchanged.

GetColumnSchema() exposes VectorBaseType (a string) and VectorDimensions (an integer) through the column indexer. Both are when the result is not reported as a vector, including a float16 column returned as varchar(max) under v1. For table or view columns, the sys.columns catalog view exposes vector_dimensions, vector_base_type, and vector_base_type_desc. Catalog visibility depends on the caller's permissions.
JSON returned by the server under v1 and JSON rendered by the driver under v2 can use different numeric notation. Compare the represented values rather than expecting identical text.

ctor1.summary: Constructs a vector with the given values.

Null.summary: Represents a null instance without any attributes.
Null.remarks: This property is provided for compatibility with DataTable. In most cases, prefer using IsNull to check if a SqlVector instance is a null vector. This is equivalent to null value.

Length.summary: Returns the number of elements in the vector.

Memory.summary: Returns the vector values as a memory region. No copies are made.

CreateNull.summary: Constructs a null vector of the given length. SQL Server requires vector arguments to specify their length even when null.
CreateNull.exception: Vector length must be non-negative, and must not exceed the vector type's maximum element count: 1998 for float32, or 3996 for float16.
